note:
One chain name, `shared`, created in BOTH an ip table and an ip6 table of the same name, and jumped to in only one of them. The ip copy is reached from its own `input`; the ip6 copy is reached by nothing at all — a v6 chain that was meant to be wired up and is not, which is the ordinary shape of this mistake in a real ruleset.

Kills the name-only-jump port: a walk that records `jumped to shared` without the (family, table) it was written in answers for both copies at once, and gets exactly one of the two answers wrong whichever way it errs — either it hides the dead v6 chain behind the live v4 one, or it reports the live one as unreachable. Both anchors are held for that reason: the point is not that the collector can say Unreferenced, it is that it DISCRIMINATES between two chains sharing a name.

nft prints the two tables' chains with identical handles (1 and 2 in each family), so a subject keyed on the handle instead of the name collapses them the same way.
anchors_note: Staged truth from the two rulesets that were loaded: the ip table got `input { jump shared }` and the ip6 table got no jump at all, so the ip copy carries JumpedFrom ['input'] and no Unreferenced, and the ip6 copy carries Unreferenced true and no JumpedFrom. Four anchors, not two, because each chain's answer is asserted in both directions — an implementation that leaked reachability across families satisfies half of this and fails the other half, and half is what tells a reader which way it is wrong. nft-tables added 2026-08-23 with the R3d port, over the same staged ruleset: 2 table(s), counted by hand off nft.json's own entries — a table entry opens a row, chains label it, rules count into it.
